newsitem.title: USA: And now, a floating Disney "theme park".
newsitem.headline: And now, a floating Disney "theme park".

text.p: The same Disney marketing machine that redefined American vacations, pushed animated videos into most middle-class living rooms and stamped mouse ears on every consumer product imaginable now wants to send you to sea.
Walt Disney Co. began accepting reservations Monday for its fledgling cruise line, which is not due to sail until April 1998.

Disney anticipates so much demand for its new cruise vacations that it's planning to hold a lottery next year to choose the winners who get to pay for berths aboard the inaugural voyage and related "celebratory sailings," according to Arthur Rodney, president of the Disney Cruise Line.
"We don't have to do much in the way of brand recognition," Rodney said in an interview at the company's 25th anniversary party for its Walt Disney World parks and resorts in central Florida.

More than 5,000 journalists from around the world and all of Disney's top brass from its California headquarters were on hand for an orgy of entertainment and Hollywood stars marking the event at the sprawling 28,000-acre Disney World.

Disney being Disney, consumers can also expect to see the new cruise line burst onto the scene with joint marketing promotions with AT&T Corp., McDonald's Corp. and American Express. Cruise advertisements are also sure to show up on the Disney cable channel, in Disney's family magazines and in theatres where Disney movies are shown.

Disney will launch its first ship, the Disney Magic, in April 1998 with three- and four-day cruises off the Florida coast. The cruises are designed as an add-on package for families and couples at Walt Disney World near Orlando.
Rodney said he anticipated adding seven-day cruises during the first year of operations "because we have so much entertainment aboard these ships."
A second ship, the Disney Wonder, is to be delivered at the end of 1998.
Cruise industry experts estimate that Disney spent more than $300 million to build each ship, plus at least $25 million to purchase and develop a private Bahamian island as a port of call.
"It's a sizable investment for the company," Rodney said, declining to give specific figures. "We're roughly equivalent to another theme park with these two ships and the island."

Rodney said the cruise line would be profitable in 1999, after its first full year of operation. "We expect to make a major contribution to this company, as well as to theme park stays, food and beverage sales and other revenue," he said.
Nearly half of the 1,000 acre private island is being developed for vacationers to swim, fish, snorkel or sunbathe, Rodney said, and Disney is also thinking of building a hotel there.

Analyst Jill Krutick of Smith Barney said the new cruise unit was part of a company-wide strategy to develop attractions and resorts that keep families on its giant Walt Disney World property -- and spending money -- for their entire vacation.
"It will enhance the length of stay patterns," she said. "It's another way of keeping people at Disney, just like another attraction at a park."
Disney Cruise Lines is charging premium prices for its packages, compared with the rest of the U.S. cruise industry, which has struggled to fill a growing number of new ships.

A seven-day resort and cruise vacation begins at $1,229 per person for a combiend cruise and a stay at Disney's moderately priced hotels, and can range as high as $3,339 per person for a cruise and a stay at Disney's luxury hotels.
Even the dining rooms aboard the ships will be different.
One room, the Animator's Palette, pays tribute to Disney animators with wall-sized sketches that first appear in black and white, but gradually add colours as the meal progresses, Rodney said.
The Disney ships will also differ from the rest of the industry by not having gambling casinos and devoting nearly a full deck to childrens' activities.

One area, the Oceaneer Club, is designed for kids aged three to eight and will offer character-themed games and a pirate ship. Another area, the Oceaneer Lab, is for nine to 12-year-olds, with interactive media and high-tech games.

"Parents will be able to sign up their kids for activities from breakfast until 1 a.m. the next day if they wish," Rodney said. "Being Disney, we have to be better than everybody else with kids' entertainment."
